messages.author: 8d7e6559e413a92b
messages.subject: Hierarchical spatial model specification advice
parts:
Hello, 

First, I should apologize for my ignorance. I have workable understanding of general bayesian approaches (glm and hierarchical models), but I am totally new to spatial modeling. I am also new to stan. 

I am trying to figure out the best approach for modeling a specific problem and I can't let go of the idea of modeling the entire problem simultaneously. I am hoping someone might be able to tell me whether stan is a suitable framework for this model, and if stan is not, perhaps an alternative could be nominated. I would also very eagerly welcome any feedback on the model I have in mind. 

My dependent variable is aggravated assault rates at the county level, so I will be using a negative binomial model. I am interested in investigating the association between county-level attitude measures. However, the attitude data is at the individual level and it is terribly distributed. Some counties have very low coverage, responses are clustered in urban areas, etc. I also would like to include a few measures that occur only at the state level. 

Ideally (I think), I would like to estimate county-level means for my attitude variables within the same model that regresses assault rates on them. My thinking is that this will preserve the uncertainty that will necessarily be associated with the attitude estimates. 

This means that I have individuals, nested in counties, nested in states. And, if I'm really honest, I'd also like to avoid collapsing items in my attitude measurements, so I would like to add an item level to the attitude measurements (i.e. I have three indicators for each dimension). So, this already seems like a pretty scary model, given that I have about 170,000 cases for the attitude measurements and about 3000 counties. On top of all of this, I need to control for spatial auto-correlation. 

The other option would be to estimate a separate model for the attitude measures and then propagate estimates from this model to the aggravated assault model. I am concerned, though, about just using point estimates for the attitude measures; so I wonder what approach could be used to ensure that the uncertainty of these measures is also included in the model. 

I should note that I read the tutorial on exact sparse CAR models in Stan. I am just unsure about how feasible it is to scale this up to the model I'm describing (remember, I'm ignorant). I've also been looking into R -INLA and, of course, I've come across WinBugs. 

Ultimately, the issue I am running into is that I can't find examples of models similar to the one I want to estimate. I don't know if that is just a coincidence, if it is because it is not feasible, or if it is because there is a much better way to go about constructing the model. 

Any and all thoughts would be welcome!

Best,
Joe Hoover

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical spatial model specification advice
parts:
We code up hierarchical models for this kind of data all the time.
The key question is how you code correlations---you can do it
with either random effects for counties, groupings of counties, or
you can literally try to do it via spatial proximity using something
like a Gaussian process (I'm not up on all the variants like CAR
and ICAR and what not). You might want to look at something like
the radon case study:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/radon.html

I'd suggest you start with simpler models and work up to a bigger
model a piece at a time.

- Bob
